passage.text:
Mural festival notice
The High Street mural festival begins Saturday at ten. Artists will paint four walls along the old market row. Visitors may watch but must stay behind the barriers. Free maps are available at the library entrance.

Text from Jake
Hey, the wall behind the sports hall is being repainted tomorrow. If you want to add your name to the design, send it to me before midnight. The artist chooses five names only.

Community board
The council has approved a new mural on the bridge wall. Work starts next month and the road stays open. Residents who live nearest the bridge will receive a letter about noise during the first week.

Art class email
Your place on the mural design course is confirmed. Bring pencils and a ruler to the first session. You do not need paint — we provide everything for the practical wall work on day two.

Shop window sign
Sorry — our front wall is being cleaned this week, so the entrance is around the side. The shop is open as usual. Please watch for wet paint near the back door until Friday.

questionGroups.instruction: For each question, choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.

passage.text: The people below want to choose from art classes, creative workshops and cultural activities. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: Weekend mural painting for confident beginners — Every Saturday morning, a local artist leads a small group on a public wall project near the bus station. Participants mix colours, learn brush techniques and contribute to a permanent neighbourhood design. All materials are provided and the session ends at one. The four-week course suits people who can commit to regular attendance.
passage.alt: A heron mural painted on a brick wall beside the bus station

passage.label: B
passage.text: Evening life drawing at the community studio — People who enjoy working after work gather every Thursday at the studio on Mill Road. A professional model poses for two hours while the tutor circulates with individual feedback. Bring your own pencils and paper; easels are available to borrow. The group welcomes all levels but is popular with those who have drawn before.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Free photography walk through the old quarter — Starting from the market square, this guided walk takes participants past hidden courtyards and decorated doorways. A photographer explains composition and light while the group captures images on phones or cameras. The route is flat and takes about ninety minutes. No booking is needed; just arrive at ten on Sunday.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Intensive weekend ceramics for experienced makers — For makers who have already worked with clay, this two-day workshop pushes your skills further. A visiting potter demonstrates glazing and kiln techniques on Saturday, and participants fire their own pieces on Sunday. The studio is outside town, so transport is essential. Materials cost extra but the kiln fee is included.

passage.label: E
passage.text: After-school drama club for under-fourteens — Young people aged ten to fourteen meet every Wednesday after school in the church hall. A drama leader runs games, improvisation and short scene work that builds confidence for shy performers. Parents collect children at five. The term fee is modest and covers a final showing for families.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Online creative writing course with weekly feedback — Flexible and self-paced, this six-week course sends a new writing prompt every Monday by email. Participants submit up to five hundred words and receive detailed tutor comments within three days. A live group chat on Friday evenings is optional. Only a computer and internet connection are required.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Monthly heritage storytelling evening at the museum — Join us on the first Friday of each month for an evening of local stories told by residents and historians. The museum provides tea and seating; attendees simply listen or share a tale of their own. Entry is free, though donations help fund the next exhibition. The hall is step-free and near the tram stop.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Daytime watercolour course for complete beginners — By the end of this five-session course, participants will have completed three small paintings suitable for framing. A patient tutor covers washes, colour mixing and simple landscapes in a bright room above the bookshop. Paper and paints are included; learners bring an apron only. Sessions run Tuesday mornings.

questions.prompt: Lena has never painted before and wants a patient morning course where everything is supplied. She hopes to take finished work home and can attend every Tuesday.
Omar is free on Saturdays, enjoys working outdoors on real walls and can commit to four weeks. He has no brushes but wants materials provided.
Priya is thirteen and quite shy. Her parents want her to try performance activities in a supportive group that meets after school and ends with a family event.
George works full-time and prefers to study from home at his own pace. He wants regular written feedback on short creative pieces and has a reliable computer.
Rosa uses a walking frame and enjoys listening to local history. She wants a free monthly event that is easy to reach by tram and does not require booking weeks ahead.

parts.passageTitle: Part 3 – The wall that changed our street

passage.text: When the council announced plans to paint the old factory wall, most residents expected another boring grey cover-up. Instead, a young artist named Dana proposed a mural showing the street's history: the bakery that once stood on the corner, the children who played hopscotch in the 1960s, and the market traders who still sell fruit on Saturdays. The council agreed, and Dana spent three weeks talking to neighbours before picking up a brush.

The painting took two months. Dana worked from a scaffold each morning while residents brought tea and watched the wall come alive. Some older neighbours corrected details — the bakery door was blue, not green — and Dana happily repainted sections. Children from the primary school added small tiles along the bottom, each showing their own dream for the street. The whole process felt more like a conversation than a construction project.

Since the mural was finished, the street has changed in ways nobody predicted. Tourists stop to photograph it, and a nearby café now opens on Sundays to serve visitors. More importantly, residents say they talk to each other more often. The wall gave them a shared story, and that story is still growing: Dana returns each summer to add a new panel based on recent neighbourhood events.

passage.text: The idea for a community garden first came up at a residents' meeting last spring. (16) ..... Many families in our street had no outdoor space of their own, and the local park was too far for elderly people to walk to every day. Several families volunteered to look after specific sections, watering the plants and pulling out weeds on a rotating schedule that everyone agreed on at the first meeting.

A local business agreed to donate soil and seeds for the first season. (17) ..... The council also gave permission to use the empty land behind the old supermarket, which had been abandoned for nearly five years and was full of weeds. We spent weekends clearing the overgrown land, removing rubbish and old tyres that had been dumped there over the years by people passing through the area.

Volunteers of all ages arrived on the first Saturday morning, ready to work. (18) ..... Some people brought tools from home, while others simply offered to make tea for the team and prepare sandwiches for lunch. The local newspaper sent a photographer to take pictures of our progress, and a short article about the garden appeared in the weekend edition with quotes from several volunteers.

By the middle of summer, the garden was full of tomatoes, lettuce and fresh herbs. (19) ..... Neighbours who had never spoken before began exchanging recipes and gardening tips, and friendships grew as quickly as the vegetables. The gardeners began sharing tips about which vegetables grew best in the local soil, and some older residents taught the younger ones how to plant seeds properly and care for them.

Now the garden has become a central part of the neighbourhood in a way nobody expected. (20) ..... We even hold outdoor cooking classes there during the warmer months, using the vegetables we have grown together. Several other streets have approached us for advice on starting their own community gardens, and we have created a simple guidebook that explains the whole process from start to finish.

passage.text: Our school organised a photography competition last month, and the response was fantastic. The rules stated that every photo (21) ..... to be taken within the town, so nobody could use holiday pictures from abroad. We had two weeks (22) ..... the deadline, which gave everyone enough time to find interesting subjects and practise their photography skills. The judges were looking for original ideas rather (23) ..... technical skill, which encouraged beginners to participate. My best picture was (24) ..... a cat sitting on an old wall in the morning sunlight, and I was surprised when it won second place in the competition. (25) ..... the winners were announced, the head teacher invited a local photographer to give a talk about his career. Many students said they (26) ..... never thought about photography as a career before that day, but the talk changed their minds. The competition also inspired several other students to take up photography as a hobby, and the art teacher started a weekly photography club that meets every Friday afternoon after lessons finish. The exhibition also gave students a chance to explain their choices to visitors. Some guests asked about camera settings, so the group prepared a short guide and displayed it beside the photographs.

passage.text: When I first joined the school book club, I was nervous because I did not know (27) ........ else who enjoyed reading as much as I did. The club met every Tuesday after school, and we took turns choosing (28) ........ book to discuss each month. My first choice was a mystery novel (29) ........ my older brother had recommended to me the previous summer. During the discussion, I was surprised to discover (30) ........ most members had already read it and loved the story. The group leader asked us to prepare three questions (31) ........ advance for each meeting to help the discussion flow. Now I look forward to Tuesdays more (32) ........ any other day of the week, and I have made some great friends through the club. Reading has become an even bigger part of my life since joining the club, and I have discovered authors I would never have found on my own without the recommendations from other members. At first I was nervous about speaking to strangers, but regular meetings made conversations easier. Now I look forward to the club because every visit gives me a new recommendation and a chance to discuss it.
